title: How Poison Ivy Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with news of the show moving offices to a Sears-era building in Atlanta (Ponce City Market) and Josh's poison ivy story from his Highlands house, where he removed a large vine and got a severe rash despite believing he was immune. They explain poison ivy's cause: urushiol, the oily compound in the sap, named after the Japanese word for lacquer, and its immune-system basis as a mistaken response (allergic contact dermatitis). They cover identification of poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac, delayed reactions, when to go to the hospital, myths about spreading the rash by scratching, first-aid washing advice, treatments like calamine and baking soda paste, barrier creams like Ivy Block, and safe removal. The episode closes with a listener mail about the state of science and the scientific method.

segments.title: Office move and poison ivy anecdote
segments.summary: Hosts announce the move to a new Atlanta office in the former Sears building at Ponce City Market. Josh recounts removing a large poison ivy vine from his yard while believing he was immune, and getting a severe rash.

segments.title: History and urushiol
segments.summary: Poison ivy was once sold as an ornamental and was briefly used in folk medicine. Majima isolated urushiol, the compound responsible for the allergic reaction, named after the Japanese word for lacquer.

segments.title: Plant family and how exposure works
segments.summary: Urushiol is found in all parts of the plant and stays potent on objects and in dead plants for years. Poison oak and poison sumac belong to the same family. Only a tiny amount is needed to cause a reaction.

segments.title: Identifying poison ivy, oak and sumac
segments.summary: The hosts describe leaf shape, the leaves-three rule, color changes by season, habitat, and how poison oak and poison sumac look different. Poison oak grows as a shrub, and sumac is a woody shrub found in swamps and along northeastern and midwestern rivers.

segments.title: Immune response and delayed reactions
segments.summary: The rash is a mistaken immune response: skin processes urushiol, T cells and macrophages attack it, and damage to tissue produces the rash. Reactions can be delayed by hours or days. Ingesting or inhaling smoke from burning plants can be dangerous, and symptoms like throat swelling require hospital care.

segments.title: Myths, washing, and treatment
segments.summary: The rash is not contagious by itself, though residual urushiol on skin or clothing can spread it. Washing with cold water quickly after exposure helps, followed by rubbing alcohol. Scratching can cause infection, not spread. Calamine, baking soda paste, oatmeal baths, and barrier creams like Ivy Block are discussed.

segments.title: Removing poison ivy safely
segments.summary: Advice on removing poison ivy: wear protective clothing, cut the vine before pulling it from the tree, pull out the roots, and do not burn it because smoke carries urushiol.

segments.title: Listener mail on science and the scientific method
segments.summary: A listener, Ian Street PhD, writes about the difficulties of current science and the value of the scientific method, following up on an earlier episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts tell listeners how to contact the show and where to find more information.
